newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission suggests ways to revitalise ACP relations.
newsitem.headline: Commission suggests ways to revitalise ACP relations.

text.p: The European Commission has put forward suggestions to revitalise relations with African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) developing countries and to make aid and trade benefits more effective.

In a discussion paper drafted ahead of the expiry of the current Lome aid and trade pact in February 2000, the Commission notes that despite four decades of European Union assistance, 41 out of the 50 poorest countries of the world are ACP states.

Their participation in international trade remains marginal and prospects of escaping from poverty are extremely worrying, the Commission said in the paper seeking reactions from all those involved in EU development aid.
The Commission plans to present proposals to the Council of Ministers in the second half of 1997 and start negotiations for a new pact with the 70 ACP states in September 1998.
The collapse of communism in eastern Europe and the ending of the so-called cold war between East and West paved the way for much closer economic and commercial ties.
The Uruguay Round world trade agreement, signed in Marrakesh in April 1994, also opened markets and encouraged freer trade.

As the 21st century looms, it is time to put EU-ACP relations on a new basis, taking account of the evolution in political and economic developments and especially a fundamental change in European thinking, the Commission's paper said,
It pointed out that the colonial hangover was finished and political responsibilities were now much clearer.
The global EU-ACP pact could be split into a series of regional accords to reflect the huge economic and political diversity of the ACP states.

Separate agreements could be drawn up with southern Africa, including South Africa, as well as with the Caribbean and Pacific countries which would respond to the specific needs of the different regions.
Alternatively, an agreement could be drawn up with the least developed ACP countries although the Commission's discussion paper said that this appeared to be politically and financially unattractive.
Other options were to keep the existing agreement but with different priorities or negotiate a global accord supplemented by bilateral deals to meet specific needs.
In the economic sector, EU aid should focus on promoting the private sector and making the ACP states more competitive so that they can play an active role in the world economy, the paper said.
Despite important trade benefits granted under the Lome convention, the ACP share of the EU market fell to 2.8 percent in 1994, from 6.7 percent in 1976.
But the EU remains the major market for ACP states, taking 40 percent of their exports.
Various options, ranging from maintenance of the status quo to a graduated reciprocal regime, are suggested.
Maintenance of the current system of non-reciprocal trade concessions could be reinforced by joint action on trading standards, patents and other measures.
Another option would be for the EU to apply the generalised system of preferences on a bilateral or multilateral basis.
An alternative scheme would involve reciprocal trade preferences in line with World Trade Organisation rules but with possible joint action on intellectual property rights and other new sectors.

The graduated reciprocal scheme would be drawn up between the EU and either individual, or groups of, ACP states and could also include joint action in new sectors, such as the environment and competition, which feature on the WTO agenda.

Regarding financial assistance, the main question is whether the EU should abandon project aid in favour of global aid packages which would distinguish between emergency and long term aid and between public and private sector aid.
The EU must also review conditions, such as efficiency and good management, attached to the aid as well as measures to make it more flexible.
The discussion paper, noting the growing number of aid conditions, suggests that the EU coordinate with other aid donors and draw up a short-list of important criteria.

It also noted that joint EU-ACP management of aid projects has limitations and other methods, which are cost efficient and encourage the beneficiary countries to use the aid effectively, should also be explored.
